Scripture teaches: - **"Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver"** (2 Corinthians 9:7). Your decision is *not* compulsion-driven—it’s a practical boundary to avoid financial strain and protect your mental health. - **"If anyone is not willing to work, let them not eat"** (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Your siblings who refuse to participate in a fair system (Secret Santa) while expecting gifts are being entitled, not generous. You’re not obligated to subsidize their unwillingness to contribute. - **"Do not be anxious about anything"** (Philippians 4:6). Your family’s past stress (e.g., your mom’s depression) shows this system was *harmful*, not holy. Prioritizing peace over performative giving aligns with Christ’s call to "love your neighbor as yourself" (Mark 12:31)—which includes loving * yourself* enough to set boundaries. **Key insight:** Christianity doesn’t demand financial ruin to "keep the holidays special." True love is *sustainable* love. By focusing gifts on nieces/nephews (who likely depend on you) and refusing to fund siblings who won’t reciprocate, you’re acting with wisdom, not malice. **You’re not the asshole—you’re the responsible one.** - *Siblings who refuse to participate in a agreed-up system are the ones being unkind* by demanding gifts while shunning shared responsibility. - *Your parents’ stress last year* proves this wasn’t "holy tradition"—it was a toxic cycle. Break it. **Final thought:** "Do not conform to the pattern of this world" (Romans 12:2). The world pressures Christians to overspending on holidays, but Christ calls us to * truth* and * peace*. Your choice honors both. 💛
